The process of testing programs has become increasingly complex and time-consuming, so we developed a new strategy that uses geometric concepts to streamline and enhance the testing process. At its core, this method relies on using points in a multidimensional space to represent different program inputs and their corresponding outputs, with a point's x-coordinate signifying an input parameter and its y-coordinate representing the output resulting from that input. With this approach, we can identify areas in the space where multiple inputs produce the same output, which is crucial for pinpointing potential issues. By analyzing these regions, developers can pinpoint specific input parameters that are likely causing problems in the code, making it easier to write effective test cases to diagnose the issues. In addition to its utility in testing, this geometric method also provides a framework for optimizing the coverage of test cases to maximize their effectiveness.

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of the shape of missing components in the p-parts of (mod p) étales abelian sheaf cohomology groups for GL(2,F)V, appearing in a previous unpublished work by Kottwitz, Reznikov, and Raghuram. The description revolves around Kummer theory, specifically the classification of certain one-dimensional commutative Cohen-Montgomery-Shaferevich O_X-modules and the definition of the Galois group action. The information is pertinent for possible applications in describing p-parts of (mod p) étales cohomology groups for various automorphic representations.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate sensing capabilities into damaged areas of structures are of great interest for condition-based structural health monitoring. A new technique called 'exact damage shaping' aims to utilize this technology to predict the precise location and size of incidents in structures through minimal initial sensing. The process involves using electrical impedance tomography to visualize damage within the structure and a genetic algorithm to calculate the incident's details. The feasibility of this method was tested on a laboratory-scale plate subject to a circular force, resulting in accurate predictions of incident locations and sizes compared to established models.

This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces based on geometric considerations, offering a novel perspective on the vector and scalar products. A detailed examination of the underlying geometry paves the way for a tensor description, revealing both the vector and scalar products to be geometric fundamentals. The paper's findings demonstrate the vector product to be a derivative of the scalar product, uncover a fundamental identity involving the vector product, and establish a geometric basis for the tensor description, all without relying on exterior algebra.

A right-angled Artin group can be viewed as a fundamental group of an associated graph's space, making this perspective a useful tool for applying topological methods to the study of these groups. Building upon previous work, we establish that for a right-angled Artin group whose associated graph has a finite tree-like subgraph, there exists a non-trivial action by left translations that induces a free and properly minimal action on a subset of the group's unitary square roots, potentially leading to a free and properly minimal action on the unitary square roots of the group's quotient by a non-trivial action by left translations in a given hyperbolic space. Moreover, we demonstrate that this free and properly minimal action is equivalent to an isomorphic free and properly minimal action found in a previous study, ensuring the applicability of previous results to the study of right-angled Artin groups in hyperbolic spaces.

The advent of big data technologies has created a pressing need to process large matrices quickly, particularly in contexts like linear regression and least squares method. In response, various techniques such as Coppersmith-Winograd (CW) and Stothers-Verron (SV) have been developed to speed up matrix multiplication, from which a inverse matrix can be derived through iteration. Our research extends these techniques to the iterative inversion of matrices, ensuring that the methods are suitable for GPU acceleration. The results show that our generalized techniques significantly improve upon existing approaches, specifically in terms of sparse matrices and real-symmetric matrices, and exhibit performance gains following the patterns observed in CW and SV, particularly in the (3\times3)-size case.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred following the pandemic, when there's a need for optimizing resource allocation in a variety of settings such as healthcare, education, and finance through real-time data that's often scarce and limited. Despite the numerous advances in the area, one major challenge remains in implementing the contextual linear bandit learning approach in a variety of settings, particularly in settings that are remote and isolated. This challenge is especially true when sharing context information is not permitted or is highly restricted, as is often the case in many real-world settings. In this research, we explore the idea of developing a contextual linear bandit learning approach that is fully decentralized and context-oblivious, using only weak assumptions that are easily satisfied. This approach utilizes a UCB-based algorithm that is context-free and a learning scheme that is gradient-based to update the action vector at each node. The key contribution of this research is the development of a new contextual linear bandit learning approach that is fully decentralized and context-oblivious. This new approach surpasses existing decentralized context-free learning methods by achieving better regret bounds without sacrificing any additional assumptions.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, the development of the VSI itself might also be influenced by the growth and settling of particles. In a effort to better understand the conditions under which VSI emerges and declines, a theoretical study was conducted examining the stability of a model system with varying levels of particle size and altitude. The results showed that the VSI can be triggered or suppressed based on the height at which particles accumulate, leading to a stability gap in areas where particles create a distinct boundary between cool, settling gas near the top and warmer, more stable gas near the bottom. The findings suggest that the type of particle size distribution might be a key factor in determining the areas of VSI occurrence in protoplanetary disks, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas as well.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of Liouville theorem, specifically on a type of manifold called Ricci shrinkers, which has a characteristic that the Ricci curvature is shrinking over time. The underlying assumption is that this kind of manifold has a uniform scalar curvature, indicating that its size is consistent across different locations. The main contribution of this paper is the establishment of a Liouville theorem, which demonstrates that there are no harmonic functions on this type of manifold that exceed certain value of a reference function called the constant multiple. The key technique employed involves utilizing the maximum principle for a type of equation called the Poisson equation, which is a linear inhomogeneous elliptic equation. The scope of this research is further expanded to the application of Liouville theorem in the stabilization of the fundamental solution to the heat equation on the aforementioned manifold.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers that activate these embedded features are static in their positioning and pattern, thus enabling detection mechanisms to function effectively. However, researchers have recently discovered methods like Neural Cleanse and ABS to be vulnerable to triggers that are dynamic, meaning they are unaffected by pattern or location, thus compromising their reliability. What is even more challenging, is that these sophisticated backdoors require an inordinate amount of compromised training data. In a breakthrough study, it has been found that even without significantly compromising training data, hidden functionalities could arise from the presence of a specific neural network architecture called the global average pooling layer, despite initial difficulty in accomplishing this feat in various machine learning tasks such as sound classification, text sentiment analysis, and image classification.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning from a distributed and heterogeneous dataset on a graph can be an efficient process. This process involves a learner node that takes random walks on the graph to gather necessary data but keeps the specific locations of the nodes unknown to the server. Under the assumption that the graph degree distribution is bounded and the number of nodes is finite, it is possible to estimate the number of times the learner visits each node during the learning process. This statistic is crucial in ensuring the convergence of optimization algorithms used in machine learning. A key benefit of this method is that it does not require knowledge of the graph structure at the server. Instead, the server can simply ask the learner for the number of visits to specific nodes, which can be answered based on the walker's memoryless property of the random walk. This approach is particularly suitable for use in privacy-enhancing scenarios such as federated learning, where sensitive information about the graph structure should remain confidential.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper proposes a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses a simple consistency framework where the segmentation model predicts boundaries between classes rather than directly predicting class labels. This approach leverages the advantages of alternative optimization techniques such as KKT conditions and reduces overfitting by incorporating more noise during optimization. The method has been tested on two publicly available datasets: MMWHS and ABIDE. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed technique in improving medical image segmentation performance compared to current methods.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing genuinely non-local tasks.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-based Federated Learning frameworks for enhancing IoVs through various applications, including Intelligent Transportation Systems, vehicle-based edge computing, and V2X communication. Furthermore, the paper outlines a novel BC-FL framework that integrates Blockchain technology with Federated Learning to enhance data privacy and security for IoVs through a smart contract-based incentive system. The review also discusses possible future applications, conditions, and challenges in implementing this technology.

A cutting-edge video identification system uses Long Short-Term Memory networks, and meeting real-time requirements while minimizing energy expenditure is challenging due to the sizeable computational needs of LSTMs. To address this challenge, a new LSTM architecture called Hierarchical Tucker Decomposition-based LSTM networks is proposed, along with a joint algorithm and hardware design that incorporates this new architecture.  A combination of low-rank Tucker decompositions on sequential input data and weight tensors is used to reduce computations and memory usage, and a corresponding hardware accelerator is designed to take advantage of these optimizations.  Compared to the state-of-the-art hardware solutions for RNNs, the proposed hierarchical Tucker decomposed LSTM network achieves higher accuracy with significantly decreased model sizes and energy consumption, and real-time video identification is achieved on a single frame of a typical HD video in about 100 milliseconds with an extremely low energy cost of 0.2 millijoules per frame.  The proposed design also outperforms the current highest performance hierarchical Tucker decomposed LSTM hardware in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and power efficiency on the Ceba-X1000 FPGA.

A positive integer p is considered prime if its only positive divisors are 1 and p. This paper offers a comprehensive discussion on prime numbers from a unique perspective, focusing on their characterization in the context of polynomial composition iterates. A key theorem proves that a number is prime if and if only if there exists a polynomial $f$ such that $p$ is the smallest positive integer for which $f(x+\theta)\neq x+\theta p$ has an integer root. Additionally, we explore the connection between prime generating polynomials and the binomial polynomial $x(x-1)$...

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions exponentially blow up in a finite time period when the nonlinearity is monotically increasing, and in a perturbed case with a small parameter, we utilize a variational identity to prove the explosion of solutions.
We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over a finitely produced $\Q$-algebra have a positive characteristic.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the issues with model fit values and the practical application of Bayesian model embedding to evaluate scenarios where multiple outcomes can result from a single experiment. We examine the challenges in assessing the underlying theoretical framework, the difficulty in accounting for prior knowledge, and the problems with Bayes factor variability in relation to Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations. We discuss various approaches to evaluating theories based on Bayes factors, including the use of Bayesian model averaging, the reliability of Bayes factor estimates, the importance of prior distribution quality, and the advantages of using existing knowledge to inform prior distributions. We conclude by emphasizing the need for a framework that can objectively evaluate the underlying theoretical principles in cognitive science, along with a proposed step-function prior distribution that can enhance the effectiveness of Bayes factor analysis in assessing theory performance in relation to data fit.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use.

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we develop a comprehensive framework that generates various types of twisted affine Lie groups. The initial application of this method yields the standard Jordanian twist functions, which serve as a foundation for deriving various alternative representations of the universal R-matrix. Furthermore, we obtain representations of the universal R-matrix that are invariant under a one-parameter subgroup of the group of diffeomorphisms, which in turn enables the derivation of classical R-matrix functions that are applicable in the context of classical exchange algebra.

This research advances the field of regular expression based constraints by introducing an innovative method for solving them using automated reasoning, particularly utilising SMT systems. Our novel approach extends the classic regular expression theory to accommodate not only unbounded regular expressions but also regular expressions with wildcard character matching, which can be specific to individual characters. The contributing authors also enhanced the existing algorithm for determining if a regular expression matches a given string, which they recast as a reachability problem on a finite automaton graph. The proposed technique enables the compilation of regular expression constraints into descriptive specifications that can be utilized for verification tools, which already employ such a framework such as liveness properties in systems of interest. The research further developed a symbolic solving method for regular expression constraints, which can be applied to constraints with multiple instances or varying instances of the wildcard character in a list of strings. The investigators conducted a series of experiments using a benchmark of 1000 unique strings with a mix of English alphabet characters and digits to evaluate the efficacy of the proposed approach in comparison to existing solutions, which included an analysis of performance in terms of memory usage and solving time for each instance.

Building upon previous work by Fitzpatrick, Kaplan and ManhÃªre and by Fitzpatrick, Kaplan, Lin, ManhÃªre and Wang, we thoroughly explore the structure of spinning operator product expansion blocks in CFT$_2$ with particular focus on their holographic counterpart within the AdS$_3$ gravity framework. Key developments include the identification of a conserved quantity, known as'spin', which distinguishes between spinning and non-spinning block operators, as well as the derivation of a conserved quantity, denoted as 'holographic spin', which plays a crucial role in solving the homogeneous wave equation in the AdS$_3$ gravity framework. Furthermore, we outline a comprehensive scheme for classifying spinning operator product expansion blocks based on their spin value, detail the computation of spinning block Witten diagrams, and provide a formula for the dimension of spinning primary operators.

To achieve high-resolution imaging with lobster-eye (LE) optics for X-rays, we need to use multiple LE mirrors in a single system. This paper discusses the concept of using LE optics in a wide-field X-ray monitoring context, where a single LE mirror can create a large, but slightly distorted, image of the sky. We propose a strategy to use multiple LE mirrors in a single system to cover a wide field of view while achieving the desired resolution. This approach is particularly suitable for a wide-field X-ray monitoring mission, which can observe a large portion of the sky by using a single LE mirror per field of view. We demonstrate the feasibility of this proposal by conducting a simulation to determine the ideal configuration of LE optics for such a mission, which would involve a array of small, deformed parabolic mirrors that can be more compact and with less material than conventional optics, resulting in less background signal from material and more sensitive detection of weak X-ray signals.

The halo model of structure formation can be challenging to apply Owen-Wang-Bertschinger (OWB) perturbation theory due to its inherent assumptions. Specifically, it may not be possible to expand the linear perturbation theory in terms of the mass fluctuation field, particularly when analyzing the halo mass function. To further complicate matters, the OWB approach cannot be applied to models that involve topological identities such as the "tubular neighborhood" condition. However, a novel approach has been proposed that involves the cosmic speed field, which might offer an alternative solution. To explore this idea, a new analytical expression was derived for the halo mass function, incorporating the linear perturbation theory of the density and velocity divergence fields. Furthermore, deep learning models were employed to accurately calculate the average squared velocity discrepancy between the model and N-body simulations for halos larger than $10^{12.5}M_{\sun}$ at redshift $z=0$. The results showed that the velocity discrepancy was negligible compared to the density discrepancy for halos smaller than $10^{13}M_{\sun}$. As a result, the expression involving the velocity field was found to be equivalent to the traditional OWB expression for this halo size range. On the other hand, the deep learning predictions indicated that the average squared velocity discrepancy could be significant for halos larger than $10^{15}M_{\sun}$. To further investigate, additional N-body simulations were conducted to analyze the velocity field

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn clusters on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of a single Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while larger clusters exhibited localized YSR state splitting. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the prediction of zero-field split YSR state energies was possible. Experimental data from photoemission spectroscopy was successfully replicated, demonstrating the theoretical model's efficacy in predicting YSR state masses and gaps for various cluster configurations.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in the 2019 ISIC challenge tasks 1 and 2, respectively. Our ensemble model combines a deep learning algorithm with an outlier detection technique, specifically using the Shannon entropy metric to identify minority classes. Initially, we trained a variety of convolutional neural networks (CNN) on the challenge dataset, then selected five top-performing models for our final ensemble. However, we noted that even with a large dataset, there are inevitably outlier samples that can negatively impact performance. Therefore, we incorporated the entropy values into our models to better identify these outliers. This technique allowed us to further enhance our results compared to using the majority class label. Ultimately, our ensemble model achieved accuracy rates of 75.1% and 85.9% for tasks 1 and 2, respectively.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as a significant component of these colliders. Within this context, a revised understanding of these colliders is developed, centering on the distribution of weak bosons and their decay products. It is determined that transverse momentum resummation and weak boson decay dynamics have a negligible impact on the underlying event formation, leading to the conclusion that treating weak bosons in a "collider physics" sense is largely unaffected by transverse momentum fluctuations. A simplified model is proposed, focusing on the distribution of weak bosons and their decay products, which demonstrates improvement over traditional underlying event simulations by reducing the amount of transverse momentum emitted beyond the weak boson radius and enhancing the simulation of large transverse momentum emissions. The development paves the way for incorporating the new underlying event simulation in matching fixed-order calculations with parton shower and time-evolving width effects, which is crucial for constructing precise theoretical predictions for high-energy lepton colliders.

We bring together Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser in a single paper to provide a concise historical perspective on their contributions to logic, mathematics, and the philosophy of language. Our gathering occurs in the present day, in a realm of formal systems defined within Peano arithmetic, where we examine the first incompleteness theorem and its implications for language, truth, and confirmation. We offer a brief biography for each figure, followed by an analysis of their key accomplishments and a discussion of their influential ideas on semantics, completeness, and the notion of truth. Moreover, we outline a formal model of truth based on their previous work, incorporating both their intuitive perspectives on truth and the formal concepts of consistency and undecidability. Our purpose is to present a unified view of their collective contributions, bypassing the need to delve into extensive historical background information.

This work investigates the concept of invariant sets in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise, straightforward proof that demonstrates there are no non-trivial invariant manifolds in general dynamical systems from a stability viewpoint. A brief extension of the argument shows that in systems where the linearized equation has constant coefficients, only the line through the equilibrium point constitutes an invariant set. A notable example illustrates how a hyperbolic linear system can feature an invariant line that isn't tangent to the eigenlines at the origin, contradicting a commonly cited statement.

This study tackles the challenge of reconstructing the interior structure of a shared box containing sound waves and air oscillations by using data from sensors placed on the structure's exterior. A new approach called "iterative local desingularization" is introduced to meet this challenge. Unlike conventional methods that rely on exact knowledge of the domain's boundaries, this iterative process can handle irregularly shaped domains and accounts for the domain's changes over time. Proof of the approach's effectiveness is provided by mathematical evidence, indicating that the reconstructed structure can be pinpointed with precision.

Within the context of a two-sided mirror symmetry, we develop a simple yet effective framework for understanding the particle dynamics. Focusing on the weak side of the symmetry, we prioritize the analysis of the weak hypercharge gauge boson's properties. Utilizing one-loop renormalization group equations, we examine both the minimal standard model extensions and the stability of the vacuum. Aiming to achieve a consistent picture, we modify the underlying framework to include a top-side hypercharge gauge boson component. Revisiting the minimal framework, we explore alternative scenarios where an additional light particle contributes to stability. Combining the analyses, we map out a stable vacuum region, predicting a dark matter relic density of approximately $10^{-12}$. To accommodate this outcome, we introduce a logarithmic divergence correction. Evaluating the framework's consistency, we verify the absence of dangerous dangerous $Z'$ mediated decays and reconcile the particle spectrum's stability with experimental results.
